fields.hero_description: Build a wellness survey that scores each area of wellbeing by team or site and saves every answer to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Makes Wellness Answers Worth Acting On
fields.features_subheading: A wellness survey measures how people are faring at work and outside it, and shows an organization which group needs support first.
fields.feature_1:
Questions grouped by area

Sorts every question under one area, such as physical, emotional, financial, or social wellbeing. Each area then gets its own average on a 1 to 5 scale for each team and site.
fields.feature_2:
Small groups stay out of view

Withholds results for any group below the answer count you choose, five for example. Those answers still feed the overall score, and no view connects a rating to a name.
fields.feature_3:
An opt-in follow-up question

Closes the survey with an optional question asking whether the person wants someone to reach out. A yes adds them to a private list for the team you name, answers attached.
fields.feature_4:
Interest checks before you spend

Asks people to pick the offerings they would use, such as a gym stipend or flexible hours. Picks are tallied by team, which sizes next year's wellness budget to real demand.
fields.feature_5:
Delivery that reaches every shift

Sends the survey by email or Slack, then reminds only those who have not answered. Drivers and floor staff with no work inbox scan a printed QR code, and replies join one table.
fields.feature_6:
The whole app, in your GitHub

Exports the survey app to your GitHub repository on paid plans, with its questions, scoring, dashboards, and response database. Host it yourself or keep editing in Emergent.

fields.tab_content_1:
Four sites, and where money worries run highest

Once a year, 520 people at a freight company rate 16 statements from 1 to 5, covering physical, emotional, financial, and social health. This year 412 replied. Financial health came in lowest at every site. Reno's 2.3 was the floor, and the HR lead read its comments before any other site's.
fields.tab_content_2:
Two picks each, counted before the budget

Before setting next year's wellness budget, an architecture practice asks all 96 staff to pick two of six offerings they would use. By Friday, 84 had answered. Flexible start times lead with 58 picks, while the gym stipend the partners expected to win drew 33. Each pick is saved with its studio team.
fields.tab_content_3:
For students who want someone to reach out

Midway through the fall term, a college emails its 1,240 first-year students a 10-question wellness check built for phones. The last, optional question asks whether they want someone from advising to get in touch. The 38 who tapped yes go on a private list for the advising team, with their replies attached.
fields.tab_content_4:
When a member rates progress 2 or lower

Thirty days after joining, each member of a fitness studio answers four questions by email, ending with progress toward the goal they set at signup. A progress rating of 2 or lower out of 5 puts the member on their coach's call list for the week. Members who rate 3 or higher stay off the list.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Wellness Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a wellness survey that people answer honestly and that leads to a change they can see.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick the areas you will measure
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down what the results will change before drafting a single question: next year's wellness budget, a new benefit, or support for one struggling site. A survey with no decision behind it collects answers nobody reads, and people notice when nothing happens.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Choose four or five areas instead of all eight dimensions SAMHSA lists. Body, mood, money, and relationships cover most workplaces. A campus survey often adds a section on sleep. Give each area three or four questions on one shared rating scale.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask about recent, concrete experience, such as how often work stress cut into sleep in the past month, instead of how someone feels in general. Keep the full survey under 20 questions, about five minutes, with one open comment box per section.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Set the smallest group whose results can be shown, such as five answers, and decide who opens each report. Site leads might see their own site while HR sees all of them. State both rules on the survey's first screen so people know before they answer.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Tell Emergent who takes part, which questions to ask, the minimum group size, and what a yes on the follow-up question should trigger. It builds the survey with its own response table and dashboards. A later change takes one more message.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Read a site against its own score from last year before ranking it against other sites. A warehouse and an office face different strains, and a raw ranking hides that. An area that scores lowest everywhere usually points to a company-wide fix.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Share the top findings and the one or two changes coming because of them, ideally within four weeks of closing. Run the same questions next year. People keep answering honestly when they can see that last year's answers moved something.

plan.angle: The top 10 is research reports (EBRI's Workplace Wellness Survey, Syracuse's National Wellbeing Survey, a USC workplace report, McKinsey's wellness trends), one survey people take, and vendor blogs that list employee wellness survey questions (Workhuman, Nailted, Leapsome, WebMD Health Services). None shows a wellness survey wired to the decision it feeds. This page defines the term up top, sorts questions by area of wellbeing, separates wellness from wellbeing, and shows four working surveys a team owns as an app: an annual employee baseline read by site, an interest check before the wellness budget is set, a campus check-in where students can ask for a follow-up, and a day-30 member check-in at a fitness studio.

claims_to_source: SAMHSA describes wellness in eight dimensions, including physical, emotional, financial, and social
EBRI's Workplace Wellness Survey, run with Greenwald Research, is an annual survey of US workers on well-being, finances, and benefits
Syracuse University's National Wellbeing Survey is an annual survey of US adults aged 18 to 64 covering wellbeing, relationships, and physical and mental health
The ACHA-National College Health Assessment is a national survey of college students' health habits, behaviors, and perceptions
Wellness usually refers to physical health, while wellbeing covers a broader set of areas, and the two words are often used interchangeably
A confidential survey links answers to identity while an anonymous survey stores no identity
Survey tools hide results for groups below a minimum number of answers
